newsitem.title: BURUNDI: BURUNDI RADIO SAYS 20 KILLED, ARMY DENIES REPORT.
newsitem.headline: BURUNDI RADIO SAYS 20 KILLED, ARMY DENIES REPORT.

text.p: Twenty villagers were killed in an attack by Hutu rebels in southeastern Burundi, state radio said on Thursday, but an army spokesman denied the report.
"After checking with the commanders, I can say nothing happened in Rutana province," said army spokesman Lieutenant-Colonel Isaie Nibizi. "I don't know where the radio got its information."
Burundi radio said 15 villagers were also taken hostage by ethnic Hutu rebels during an attack in Rutana province of Gitanga commune, 140 km from Bujumbura, on Wednesday.
The radio also reported violence in Bujumbura, where four people were wounded in a grenade attack on Cibitoke, a troubled district of the capital. Gunshots were also heard.
"There is a military operation underway in Muahuta commune in rural Bujumumbura," said Nibizi. "What is happening is our military is pursuing the rebels to clear them from the area."
In Brussels, Burundi's Foreign Minister Luc Rukingama said the country's warring factions would meet in Geneva next month for a peace conference to prepare talks to end civil war.

"It is not negotiations. It is a preparatory meeting for negotiations. It will be the first time when all groups in Burundi...will meet to discuss peace," he told a news conference. He was due to meet Belgian and European Union officials.

Rukingama said the meeting would be a follow-up to the "discreet phase" of the peace process -- talks in Rome earlier this month with the Hutu rebel National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD).
The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) has invited Burundi's military ruler Pierre Buyoya to its summit in Harare in June, his spokesman said earlier in Bujumbura.
"He received the invitation and he is going," said Sebastian Nthahuga, spokesman for the Tutsi military ruler who seized power from Burundi's Hutu civilian president in a coup last July.
"Without doubt he will participate as president of the Republic of Burundi. That is the meaning of this invitation."
Nthahuga said Buyoya would raise at the annual summit regional sanctions against Burundi imposed shortly after the coup last year. His goal was for them to be lifted entirely.
The regional leaders eased sanctions against Burundi last month and invited Buyoya to their summit in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha, where he was addressed as president.
Nthahuga said Buyoya wanted support at the OAU meeting from June 2 to 4 for his government's talks with the CNDD.
The talks have been met by opposition from some Tutsis, who accuse the Hutus of being genocidal killers.
"We need the support of the continent, of other African countries, and the international community," Nthahuga said.

Burundi's Tutsi-dominated army arrested 14 students on Wednesday during a university sit-in protest against Buyoya's decision to negotiate with the rebels. Both sides signed a pre-ceasefire agreement after their secret talks in Rome.
More than 150,000 people have been killed in massacres and civil war since October 1993, when the country's first elected Hutu president was murdered by Tutsi troops.
